k-1.x_notes: Identical to Y in text and diagrams; the only image differences are one-level anti-aliasing changes in a few pixels. Strengths: six concrete, actual-size problems that keep K-1 busy for the whole working time. P1 has possible and impossible boards with blues, including an even-area trapezoid with 5 up and 3 down triangles that cannot be tiled. P2 asks for the fewest greens in triangles of side 2, 3 and 4 (answers 2, 3, 4). P3 and P6 ask for all tilings of the 1-1-1, 2-1-1 and 1-2-2 hexagons (2, 3 and 6 tilings, with spare shapes). P4 asks for the fewest blocks (3, 3, 4; the trapezoid cannot be done with 3 because three chevrons would have 6 up and 6 down triangles against the board's 7 and 5). P5 is a blue-block placement game whose answers vary (first, second, first, first, second). The pages are clean and in the organizer's format. Weaknesses: kindergartners cannot write the 'say why' for P1, so an adult has to take it orally. P3 and P6 repeat the same 'find all ways' idea.
k-1.y_notes: Same packet as X: the text is identical and the page images match except for sub-visible anti-aliasing. The same strengths apply (enough concrete, correct, actual-size work for 40 minutes, including the game and the fewest-blocks problem), and so do the same weaknesses (written 'say why' for non-writers, some repetition between P3 and P6).
k-1.reason: The two K-1 packets are the same in content and layout, so there is nothing to choose between them.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Byte-identical to Y (all page images and text). Strengths: a well-sequenced, correct coloring-obstruction unit. In P1, the star has a forced tiling, the side-3 triangle has odd area, the even-area trapezoid has 7 up and 5 down triangles, and the 2-1-1 hexagon tiles. In P2, two same-type holes make the board impossible, the bowtie is balanced but still impossible, and the board with one up hole and one down hole tiles. P3 asks for the fewest greens in triangles of side 2 to 5 (n) and for a proof. P4 generalizes to side 10 and side 100. P5 compares chevrons with blues: the chevron minimums are 4, 5, 4, 5 against 2, 3, 4, 5, never fewer. P6 asks children to invent a 20-triangle board that needs 6 greens, which is feasible. P7 asks for the rule for two greens on a side-2 hexagon: one up and one down is exactly right, since all 144 such placements tile. Boards are at actual size, with enough writing space. Weaknesses: there is a lot of 'explain why' writing, P4 is abstract and shares a page with P5, and there is a fair amount of reading for 2nd graders.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Byte-identical to X, so it has the same strengths (rich, correct sequence from possible and impossible boards to proofs, invention, and the two-hole rule) and the same weaknesses (heavy written explanation, some reading load).
grades-2-3.reason: The grades 2-3 packets are identical files.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Identical to Y except for P4 and P6. Shared strengths: a strong kernel-2 arc. P1 and P2 cover the six tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon and their flip graph, whose diameter is 4. P3 has flip-distance tasks on the side-2 hexagon: I decoded the pictures and verified the distances A to B = 3, C to D = 4, E to F = 8 (E and F are the extreme tilings). P4 is about round-trip parity, P5 introduces ribbons, P6 asks for the parity proof and the lower bound of 8, P7 asks for all 20 tilings, and P8 counts the 1-3-3 hexagon (20). Boards are at actual size. Shared weaknesses: long procedural text for P5, a lot of writing (P6 is a full page of lines), and a redundant redraw in P2. X-specific: P4 starts from covering A, which I verified has three pairwise-disjoint flippable hexagons, so a 4-flip round trip with no immediate repeat exists. This is concrete and continues directly from P3. X's P6 asks children to find the fewest E-to-F flips and prove no one can do fewer. This is self-contained and robust even if a child's P3 answer was not optimal, though it partly repeats P3.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Same shared strengths and weaknesses as X. Y-specific: P4 says 'start with any covering.' This is more open, but the round trip is impossible from the two extreme 'box' coverings (E and F), because each has only one flippable hexagon. Those are exactly the tilings a child is most likely to build first, so some children may get stuck without understanding why. Y's P6 asks children to explain why no one can beat 'your answer' from P3. That presumes the child's P3 answer was the true minimum of 8; if a child found 10, the prompt asks them to justify something false.
grades-4-5.reason: The packets differ only in two prompts. X's anchored start for P4 (verified to work) and its self-contained 'find the fewest and prove it' for P6 are slightly more robust than Y's 'any covering', which fails from the extreme tilings, and Y's 'fewer than your answer'.

overall.reason: K-1 and grades 2-3 are the same in both packets, and both are mathematically sound, concrete and well sized. The only real differences are two prompt wordings in grades 4-5, where X's versions are slightly more concrete and less likely to send a child the wrong way, so X gets a slight overall preference.
